definition: A phased process for planning, building, testing, deploying, and maintaining a software system.
wrongs: A coding standard that limits line length and comment style.
A single test that proves every requirement before design starts.
A meeting cadence used only to estimate the next day's tasks.
why: The life cycle names the stages a software product passes through from an idea to ongoing upkeep.
example: A library catalog is specified, designed, coded, tested, launched for fall term, and then patched.
scenario: A campus app moves from a signed specification into design, coding, a test lab, and launch. Which overall process are these stages part of?
scenarioWhy: Those ordered stages are the software development life cycle, not one test or meeting.

definition: The work of eliciting, analyzing, specifying, and controlling what stakeholders need a system to do.
wrongs: Rewriting modules after release so they run on a new operating system.
Drawing only the physical servers a system will be installed on.
Measuring defects found per thousand lines after the final test.
why: Requirements engineering produces and manages an agreed statement of stakeholder needs before and during construction.
example: Analysts interview registrars, write the enrollment needs, and track a new grading rule.
scenario: Clinic stakeholders disagree about portal behavior and nothing is written down. Which discipline should the team apply first?
scenarioWhy: Unclear, unrecorded needs are resolved by eliciting and specifying requirements.

definition: A statement of a specific behavior or service the system must perform for its users.
wrongs: A constraint on speed, security, or uptime that does not name a user task.
A developer's estimate of hours left in the current iteration.
A diagram that shows classes but not what the system must do.
why: A functional requirement states a function the system must carry out, such as recording or calculating something.
example: The shop system must let a clerk apply a percentage discount at checkout.
scenario: The statement says a nurse can record a patient's temperature in the chart. Which kind of requirement is that?
scenarioWhy: Recording a temperature is a behavior the system must provide, so it is functional.

definition: A quality constraint, such as performance, security, reliability, or usability, rather than a user task.
wrongs: A description of a concrete action the system must carry out, such as checkout.
A user account that is allowed to approve a release.
A source file that configures the build pipeline.
why: Non-functional requirements constrain how well the system performs its functions, not which functions exist.
example: The shop system must stay available 99.9 percent of scheduled opening hours.
scenario: The catalog must answer a search in under one second for 500 concurrent users. Which kind of requirement is that?
scenarioWhy: A response-time limit is a performance quality, not a named user function.

definition: A description of how an actor reaches a goal with the system, including the main flow and alternatives.
wrongs: A set of inputs and an expected output used to verify one function.
A class operation that stores data without describing a user goal.
A time-boxed iteration that delivers a product increment.
why: A use case organizes a goal around an actor's main success path and the alternate paths that can occur.
example: Actor Customer completes Place Order, with an alternate flow when the card is declined.
scenario: The analyst writes the main steps and the card-declined alternative for Place Order. Which artifact is that?
scenarioWhy: A goal, an actor, a main flow, and alternatives are the parts of a use case.

definition: A short requirement from a user's perspective naming who wants a capability and why it matters.
wrongs: A legally frozen specification that forbids any change after sign-off.
A sequence of messages drawn between objects for one runtime scenario.
A count of branches a test suite has executed.
why: The usual story form names the role, the desired capability, and the benefit that makes it valuable.
example: As a commuter I want to see the next bus so that I can decide whether to wait.
scenario: A card reads: As a student I want to reset my password so I can reach my courses. Which requirement form is this?
scenarioWhy: The role-capability-benefit wording is the standard form of a user story.

definition: A standard visual language for modeling the structure and behavior of a software system.
wrongs: A compiled language used to implement embedded device drivers.
A repository format that stores only binary build artifacts.
A test level that runs the finished system at the customer's site.
why: UML defines standard diagram types so different teams can read the same structural and behavioral models.
example: A course handout uses standard class and sequence diagrams so two colleges can read one design.
scenario: An architect must show structure and behavior in a notation other schools will recognize. Which notation fits?
scenarioWhy: UML is the standard modeling notation for software structure and behavior.

definition: A UML structure view of classes, their attributes and operations, and relationships among them.
wrongs: A time-ordered view of messages sent between objects for one scenario.
A picture of actors and the goals they trigger.
A map of which servers host each deployed component.
why: Class diagrams model static structure: types, members, and links such as association and inheritance.
example: The diagram shows Student, Course, a grade attribute, and an enrollment association.
scenario: The designer must show Order, Customer, their fields, and a one-to-many association. Which diagram fits?
scenarioWhy: Classes, attributes, and associations are shown on a class diagram.

definition: A UML behavior view that shows messages among objects in time order for one scenario.
wrongs: A static view of classes, fields, and inheritance only.
A chart of project tasks and their calendar dates.
A table that lists requirements and their source stakeholders.
why: Lifelines run down the page and messages are ordered from top to bottom, so time is explicit.
example: The drawing shows the browser calling the API, then the API calling the payment gateway.
scenario: Reviewers want the order of calls among the cart, payment service, and bank during checkout. Which diagram fits?
scenarioWhy: A sequence diagram is the UML view that orders messages among participants.

definition: A UML diagram of actors outside a system and the goals those actors pursue with it.
wrongs: A diagram of database tables and the foreign keys that join them.
A chart that shows state changes inside one object.
A drawing of network cables between physical machines.
why: Use case diagrams summarize scope by connecting external actors to the use cases inside the system boundary.
example: The picture shows a Librarian stick figure connected to Lend Book and Return Book.
scenario: The sponsor wants a picture of the registrar and the goals Register and Drop Course. Which diagram fits?
scenarioWhy: Actors and their goals are the content of a use case diagram.

definition: A UML diagram of an object's states and the events that cause transitions between those states.
wrongs: A diagram that lists actors and the goals they trigger.
A view that shows only package dependencies at compile time.
A timeline of staff assignments across project phases.
why: The diagram names states and labels each transition with the event that causes the object to change state.
example: A traffic-light object moves from Green to Yellow to Red when a timer event fires.
scenario: An order can be New, Paid, or Cancelled, and Pay moves New to Paid. Which diagram shows that?
scenarioWhy: States and event-triggered transitions are modeled by a state machine diagram.

definition: A linear life-cycle model in which each phase is finished and baselined before the next phase begins.
wrongs: An iterative model that ships a working increment every few weeks.
A risk-driven cycle that repeats prototyping until major risks drop.
A board method that limits work in progress and has no phase gates.
why: Waterfall proceeds in one direction, so a later phase starts only after the previous phase is complete.
example: The city contract finishes the full requirements book before the vendor may start design.
scenario: The contract says design cannot start until every requirement is signed, and testing waits until coding ends. Which model is this?
scenarioWhy: Strict phase gates with no overlap are the defining rule of the waterfall model.

definition: An iterative approach that delivers working software in short cycles and expects requirements to change.
wrongs: A contract style that freezes the full specification before any code is written.
A hardware procurement process for buying servers in one batch.
A testing technique that inspects every source line exactly once.
why: Agile values working software and response to change over following a frozen plan in one long pass.
example: A lab team demos a working attendance feature every second Friday and reshuffles the next goals.
scenario: The team ships a usable slice every two weeks and revises the backlog when clinic rules change. Which approach is this?
scenarioWhy: Short deliveries plus welcomed change are the core of an agile approach.

definition: An agile framework that organizes delivery into sprints with defined roles, events, and artifacts.
wrongs: A linear sequence of phases that cannot return to an earlier phase.
A modeling language for drawing classes and sequences.
A document standard for writing IEEE requirements specifications.
why: Scrum fixes the accountabilities, events, and artifacts used to plan and inspect each sprint.
example: The product owner orders the backlog, and the team inspects a done increment at the sprint review.
scenario: The team has a product owner, a scrum master, and a two-week sprint ending in a review. Which framework is this?
scenarioWhy: The product owner, scrum master, sprint, and review are Scrum's framework elements.

definition: A Scrum iteration of one month or less that turns chosen backlog items into a releasable increment.
wrongs: The full multi-year contract from project start through retirement.
A permanent branch that is never merged back to the main line.
A customer sign-off meeting held only once at the end of the project.
why: Each sprint is a fixed timebox that produces an increment the team could release.
example: From March 1 to March 14 the team finishes password reset and could ship that increment.
scenario: The team takes 14 days to turn selected backlog items into an increment it could release. Which timebox is that?
scenarioWhy: A fixed Scrum iteration that yields a releasable increment is a sprint.

definition: A flow method that visualizes work and limits how many items may be in progress at once.
wrongs: A time-boxed iteration with a fixed sprint goal and a sprint review.
A risk model that adds a prototype at the end of every spiral loop.
A test phase that executes only after all coding is complete.
why: Kanban manages flow by making the work visible and capping work in progress on the board.
example: The support board stops pulling new tickets into Build while three tickets already sit there.
scenario: The board allows only three items in the Test column, and work is pulled when a slot opens. Which method is this?
scenarioWhy: A visible board plus a work-in-progress limit is Kanban flow control.

definition: An agile method that emphasizes pair programming, test-first development, and very frequent releases.
wrongs: A sequential model that completes all design before any programming.
A modeling language for drawing classes and sequences.
A life-cycle model shaped like a V of matched test phases.
why: Extreme Programming pushes engineering practices such as pair programming and test-first coding to a continuous rhythm.
example: Alex and Priya share one keyboard, write the test first, and integrate before lunch.
scenario: Two developers write a failing test, code together at one machine, and integrate several times a day. Which method is this?
scenarioWhy: Pair programming, test-first coding, and frequent integration are Extreme Programming practices.

definition: A life-cycle model that builds and delivers the system as a series of partial, usable releases.
wrongs: A model that waits to deliver anything until every feature is finished.
A model whose every loop is driven by a formal risk analysis.
A model that pairs each design step with a matching test level on a V.
why: Each increment adds a usable subset of function instead of holding all function for one final delivery.
example: Release 1 is course search, release 2 adds waitlists, and both stay in use.
scenario: The library system first releases search, later releases holds, and later releases fines, each usable alone. Which model is this?
scenarioWhy: Delivering usable partial systems in succession is the incremental model.

definition: A risk-driven life-cycle model that repeats planning, risk analysis, engineering, and evaluation.
wrongs: A strictly one-pass sequence with no return to earlier work.
A board that only limits work in progress and ignores risk.
A test strategy that executes white-box tests before any requirements exist.
why: Each spiral loop is planned around the biggest remaining risks, which may call for a prototype or other mitigation.
example: Loop 2 focuses on payment-fraud risk and ends with a throwaway security prototype.
scenario: Each loop starts by listing risks, and the team prototypes only the highest risk. Which model is this?
scenarioWhy: Explicit risk analysis at the start of every loop identifies the spiral model.

definition: A life-cycle model that pairs each development phase with a corresponding test phase.
wrongs: A model whose loops are sized by identified project risks.
A flow board with columns and work-in-progress limits.
A method that delivers a usable slice before the requirements are written.
why: The V pairs early specifications with later tests, such as requirements with acceptance testing and design with integration testing.
example: When the team writes the high-level design, they also plan the integration tests that will check it.
scenario: Acceptance tests are planned when user needs are specified, and unit tests are planned with detailed design. Which model is this?
scenarioWhy: Matching each development phase to a test phase is the structure of the V-model.

definition: Testing the smallest pieces of a program, such as functions or classes, apart from the rest of the system.
wrongs: Testing the finished product with the customer to decide acceptance.
Retesting the whole release only after it is already in production.
Reviewing a design document without executing any code.
why: A unit test isolates one small piece so a failure points at that piece rather than at the whole system.
example: calculateTax(100, 0.05) is executed alone and expected to return 5.
scenario: A developer checks calculateFine with inputs 3 and 7 and no database connected. Which test level is this?
scenarioWhy: One function exercised in isolation is a unit test.

definition: Testing whether separately built modules work correctly when they are connected.
wrongs: Testing one function in isolation with all collaborators replaced.
Checking spelling in the user manual before release.
Measuring only the server's power use under load.
why: Integration tests target the interfaces between modules that passed their own unit tests.
example: The order service and the inventory service are tested together when a book is sold.
scenario: Search works alone and the database works alone, but the team now checks search through the real driver. Which test level is this?
scenarioWhy: Combining modules that already work separately is integration testing.

definition: Testing the complete integrated system against its specified requirements.
wrongs: Testing a single class with mocked dependencies.
A code review that never runs the software.
Checking only that two modules compile in the same project.
why: System testing evaluates the whole product in a production-like setting against the requirements specification.
example: Testers run the entire banking app, from login through transfer, against the requirements.
scenario: Testers run the full bookstore application against the written requirements on a production-like server. Which test level is this?
scenarioWhy: Exercising the complete system against its specification is system testing.

definition: Testing that determines whether the system meets the customer's needs and can be accepted.
wrongs: Testing private methods by reading branch coverage reports.
A developer check that a function returns quickly on a laptop.
Comparing two design diagrams for matching class names.
why: Acceptance testing is the customer's decision point, based on agreed scenarios rather than internal structure.
example: Branch managers execute the agreed teller scenarios and sign the acceptance form.
scenario: Librarians run the agreed scenarios on the new catalog and decide whether to take the system. Which test level is this?
scenarioWhy: The customer's go or no-go decision against agreed scenarios is acceptance testing.

definition: Retesting existing behavior after a change to confirm that working features still work.
wrongs: The first test of a brand-new feature that never existed before.
A review of requirements text before any code is written.
Deleting old tests so the suite runs only the newest case.
why: A change can break unchanged behavior, so regression tests rerun the old checks after the change.
example: After the interest-rate fix, the old savings-account tests are run again.
scenario: After a discount fix, the team reruns the old checkout tests to see whether unchanged rules still pass. Which testing is this?
scenarioWhy: Rerunning existing tests after a change to guard old behavior is regression testing.

definition: Testing from specified inputs and outputs without looking at the internal code.
wrongs: Testing that requires the source, branches, and internal paths.
A static review that never supplies inputs to the running system.
Measuring how many developers edited a file.
why: Black-box tests are derived from the specification, so the tester does not need the implementation.
example: The tester tries valid and invalid ages from the spec and never opens the function.
scenario: The tester follows the login specification and never opens the source file. Which testing approach is this?
scenarioWhy: Using only the specification, with no view of the code, is black-box testing.

definition: Testing designed from the internal structure, branches, and logic of the code.
wrongs: Testing that uses only the requirements and ignores the implementation.
A customer demo that checks satisfaction, not code paths.
Counting story points completed in a sprint.
why: White-box tests are chosen to exercise internal paths such as both sides of a branch.
example: The tester forces the true and false sides of the overdraft condition in the source.
scenario: The tester picks inputs that force both branches of an if statement inside the source. Which testing approach is this?
scenarioWhy: Choosing inputs from the internal branches is white-box testing.

definition: A specified set of preconditions, inputs, steps, and expected results for one behavior.
wrongs: The production defect report written after users find a failure.
The schedule of who runs tests on which day.
A library binary that is linked into the program under test.
why: A test case is executable only when the setup, the action, and the expected result are all stated.
example: Precondition: balance 40. Action: withdraw 100. Expected: refusal and balance still 40.
scenario: The note says: precondition logged out, input a bad password, expect an error message. Which artifact is this?
scenarioWhy: Preconditions, inputs, and an expected result define a test case.

definition: A system that records file history so people can compare changes, branch, and restore earlier versions.
wrongs: A compiler option that removes unused functions from a binary.
A meeting where the team accepts the product increment.
A diagram that shows states of one business object.
why: Version control stores successive revisions so any earlier state of the files can be inspected or restored.
example: A developer compares today's main.c with the revision from last April to find the bad edit.
scenario: The team needs every past revision of main.c so yesterday's bug can be compared with last month. Which system provides that history?
scenarioWhy: Recorded revisions that can be compared and restored come from version control.

definition: An independent line of development in a repository that can later be merged with another line.
wrongs: The unique number a compiler assigns to each machine instruction.
A test input that is outside the allowed range.
The final approved build that customers are running.
why: A branch lets one line of commits diverge from another until the team merges them.
example: The receipts feature lives on receipts-feature until it is merged on Friday.
scenario: A developer implements refunds on a separate line of commits that is not yet in main. Which version-control concept is that line?
scenarioWhy: A diverging line of commits that can later merge is a branch.

definition: A version-control clash in which overlapping edits cannot be combined without a person choosing the result.
wrongs: A failed unit test caused by a null input.
Two requirements that describe the same user goal in different words.
A sprint that ends before all selected stories are done.
why: When two commits change the same lines, the tool stops because it cannot know which text should remain.
example: Git stops because both commits changed the same three lines of Price.java.
scenario: Two people edited the same lines of Cart.java and the tool cannot combine the commits. Which problem must they resolve?
scenarioWrongs: A syntax error in a library
scenarioWhy: Overlapping edits that cannot be combined automatically are a merge conflict.

definition: The practice of merging changes into a shared mainline often, then building and testing automatically.
wrongs: Waiting until the end of the project to combine every developer's work once.
Manually copying source files onto a server with no automated test.
Freezing requirements so no further merges are allowed.
why: Frequent integration plus an automated build and test finds merge and test failures soon after they are introduced.
example: A push to main triggers the server to compile the repo and run 800 unit tests.
scenario: Every push to the shared mainline starts a build and the unit tests on a server. Which practice is this?
scenarioWhy: Merging often and automatically building and testing is continuous integration.

definition: A document that records the agreed functional and non-functional requirements the system must meet.
wrongs: The source-code repository that holds the implementation.
A test log that lists only the cases that failed yesterday.
A budget spreadsheet of salaries for the development team.
why: The specification is the agreed baseline of what the system must do and how well it must do it.
example: The signed specification says the kiosk shall print a receipt and respond within two seconds.
scenario: The binder lists every function and quality the registrar system must meet, and both sides signed it. Which document is this?
scenarioWhy: A signed list of required functions and qualities is a software requirements specification.

definition: The ability to follow a requirement to the design, code, and tests that satisfy it, and back to its origin.
wrongs: The speed at which a team finishes story points in one sprint.
A backup copy of the database taken every night.
The practice of writing code before any requirement is recorded.
why: Trace links show that each requirement is implemented and tested, and show where a requirement came from.
example: Requirement PAY-4 links to design paragraph 3.2, class Payment, and test T-19.
scenario: An auditor follows requirement R12 from the specification to the design section, the class, and the covering test. Which ability is that?
scenarioWhy: Following a requirement through design, code, and tests is requirements traceability.

definition: A named, reusable description of a proven solution to a recurring software design problem.
wrongs: A one-time hack that works only for a single bug in one program.
A programming language keyword that declares a loop.
A customer signature on the acceptance test report.
why: A pattern names a problem, a solution structure, and the consequences so teams can reuse a known design.
example: Instead of an ad-hoc global logger, the team applies a published pattern with a known structure.
scenario: The team reuses a known design for notifying every view when the model changes, instead of a one-off. What are they reusing?
scenarioWhy: A named, proven solution to a recurring design problem is a design pattern.

definition: A creational pattern that ensures a class has only one instance and a single global access point.
wrongs: A pattern in which an object notifies many dependents when its state changes.
A pattern that lets subclasses choose which concrete class to instantiate.
A split of an application into model, view, and controller parts.
why: The singleton hides construction and returns the same instance on every request.
example: Every module asks AppLogger.getInstance() and receives the same logger object.
scenario: The application must have exactly one configuration object, reached from anywhere in the process. Which pattern fits?
scenarioWhy: One shared instance with a global access point is the singleton pattern.

definition: A behavioral pattern in which a subject automatically notifies registered dependents when it changes.
wrongs: A pattern that allows only one instance of a class in the process.
A pattern that adapts one interface so another class can call it.
A pattern that builds a complex object step by step.
why: Dependents register with the subject, so the subject can update them without hard-coding each dependent.
example: The scoreboard, the phone app, and the ticker all refresh when MatchScore changes.
scenario: When the stock price changes, every open dashboard must update without the price object naming each screen. Which pattern fits?
scenarioWhy: Automatic notification of registered dependents is the observer pattern.

definition: A creational pattern that lets subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate.
wrongs: A pattern that guarantees one shared instance for the whole program.
A pattern that forwards a call through a chain until one handler accepts it.
A pattern that saves and restores an object's state without exposing internals.
why: The creator defines the creation step, and each subclass overrides it to return its own product class.
example: ButtonFactory.create() returns a WinButton or a MacButton depending on the subclass.
scenario: The desktop subclass creates a window dialog and the mobile subclass creates a touch dialog through the same creation method. Which pattern fits?
scenarioWhy: Letting each subclass choose the concrete product is the factory method.

definition: An architectural pattern that separates application data, the user interface, and input handling.
wrongs: A network stack with seven layers from physical media up to applications.
A database rule that every table must have a foreign key.
A test method that checks only private functions.
why: The model holds state, the view presents it, and the controller interprets user input.
example: The grades model holds numbers, the page renders them, and the controller handles the Save click.
scenario: Invoice data stays in one part, the screen layout in another, and button actions in a third. Which pattern is this?
scenarioWhy: Separating data, presentation, and input handling is the model-view-controller split.

definition: The degree to which one module depends on the details or changes of another module.
wrongs: The degree to which elements inside one module all serve a single purpose.
The number of users who can log in at the same time.
The time a team spends in code review each week.
why: Coupling measures interdependence between modules; a change in one can force a change in the other when coupling is high.
example: ReportPrinter fails to compile when Invoice changes a private field that the printer reads.
scenario: Module A will not compile unless it reads private fields inside module B. Which property between the modules is high?
scenarioWhy: Dependence on another module's private details is high coupling.

definition: The degree to which responsibilities inside one module belong together and serve one purpose.
wrongs: The degree to which one module depends on the internals of another.
The count of defects found after release.
The number of branches in the version-control history.
why: A highly cohesive module has elements that all contribute to one responsibility.
example: InvoiceFormatter only formats invoice lines and totals, with no login or shipping code inside.
scenario: A module named Report contains only methods that format one sales report. Which property inside that module is high?
scenarioWhy: Elements that all serve one purpose make the module highly cohesive.

definition: Work done after delivery to correct faults, adapt to change, or improve the system.
wrongs: The first workshop that gathers requirements before any design.
Writing the initial architecture before coding starts.
Estimating the budget only for the first release.
why: Maintenance begins once the system is in use and includes corrective, adaptive, and perfective changes.
example: After launch, the city app is updated because the recycling calendar rules changed.
scenario: Three months after go-live, engineers change the payroll system so it handles a new tax form. Which life-cycle activity is this?
scenarioWhy: Changing a delivered system to meet a new condition is software maintenance.

definition: Changing internal structure to make code easier to understand or modify without changing its behavior.
wrongs: Adding a new user-visible feature while altering results the user sees.
Rewriting the system in another language and changing its outputs.
Deleting tests so a failing build becomes green.
why: Refactoring preserves observable behavior, which existing tests can confirm, while improving structure.
example: A long checkout method is split into three methods and the receipt output stays identical.
scenario: The developer splits a 400-line method into smaller methods and every existing test still passes with the same outputs. Which activity is this?
scenarioWhy: A structure change that keeps external behavior the same is refactoring.

definition: The extra future cost created when a team takes a design or code shortcut instead of a cleaner solution.
wrongs: The money a customer still owes on a software license.
The count of servers needed to host the application.
The interest rate used in a project cost-benefit spreadsheet.
why: The shortcut saves time now but adds rework later, which is the debt that must be repaid.
example: Hard-coded tax rates shipped for a demo, and every new region now needs awkward special cases.
scenario: The team skipped input checks to hit a demo, and every later feature costs extra time to work around that shortcut. What has the team incurred?
scenarioWhy: Extra future rework caused by a shortcut is technical debt.

definition: An examination of a proposed source change by other developers before it is merged.
wrongs: An automated load test that measures response time only.
The customer's final decision to accept the whole system.
A backup of the repository stored off site.
why: Reviewers read the change to find defects and design problems while the change is still unmerged.
example: Sam comments on an unhandled empty cart in the pull request before it merges.
scenario: Before the refund change joins main, two teammates read the diff and comment on a missing null check. Which practice is this?
scenarioWhy: Developers examining a proposed change before merge are doing a code review.

definition: The degree to which a system meets stated requirements and satisfies stakeholder needs in use.
wrongs: The number of lines of code written during a sprint.
The salary band of the most senior programmer.
The brand of compiler used to build the product.
why: Quality is judged by conformance to requirements and by fitness for the stakeholders' actual use.
example: The clinic rates the portal by correctness against the spec and by how easily nurses finish a visit.
scenario: Evaluators ask how completely the grading system meets the specification and how well faculty can use it. What are they judging?
scenarioWhy: Meeting the specification and satisfying users in use is software quality.

definition: Checking that a phase's work product conforms to the specification for that phase.
wrongs: Checking that the finished system fulfills the real needs of its users.
Publishing the software to an app store.
Assigning story points to items on the backlog.
why: Verification asks whether the product of a phase was built to that phase's specification.
example: The inspection checks that the module design satisfies the design description in section 4.
scenario: Reviewers compare the design document with the design specification and do not yet ask whether students like the product. Which check is this?
scenarioWhy: Comparing a work product with its phase specification is verification.

definition: Checking that the finished system fulfills the users' actual needs in their environment.
wrongs: Checking that a design document matches the design specification, regardless of user needs.
Counting how many unit tests exist, without running the product for users.
Archiving old requirements that were rejected.
why: Validation asks whether the right product was built for the users, not only whether a phase met its spec.
example: Pilots use the new departure screen on a live gate to see if it fits their real workflow.
scenario: Students try the finished registration system during advising week to see if it supports how they actually enroll. Which check is this?
scenarioWhy: Trying the finished system against real user needs is validation.

definition: Building an early, partial version so people can explore requirements or design choices.
wrongs: The final hardened release that is maintained for years.
A formal proof that every requirement has a passing test.
Locking the repository so no further commits are allowed.
why: A prototype is built to learn from users or to test a design, and it may later be discarded or evolved.
example: A clickable seat map with fake data is shown to riders before any booking code is written.
scenario: The team builds a clickable screen with fake data so nurses can react before the real database exists. Which practice is this?
scenarioWhy: An early partial version used to learn about needs or design is a prototype.

definition: Identifying software items and controlling their versions, changes, and relationships over time.
wrongs: Choosing the office layout for the development team.
A one-time compile that keeps no record of which sources produced the binary.
Writing user stories without recording which version they belong to.
why: Configuration management makes each build identifiable and reproducible from controlled versions of its items.
example: Build 4.2 is recorded as commit a1b2c3 plus library set L7 so it can be rebuilt later.
scenario: The release engineer records exactly which source revision, libraries, and build script produced build 4.2. Which discipline is this?
scenarioWhy: Identifying and controlling the exact items that make a build is configuration management.
